# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
Sections 1–5 are a valuable correction. The new findings from the microdata are real and important. Sections 6–8 then overcorrect. The conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" isn't supported by the comment's own numbers. It also leaves out the one randomised result that directly contradicts it, Varden's case-processing stratum.

The arithmetic in Table 2 checks out:
- 95.1 ÷ 0.8 gives +18.9%.
- 98.4 ÷ 0.859 gives +14.6%.
- 95.4 ÷ 0.861 gives +10.8%.
- The real-revenue figure is also right: 1.014 ÷ 1.041 is about −2.6%.

## What the comment establishes

- **Attrition was misreported.** This is the most serious finding. The working paper says the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show seven of the nine left after the schedule began, mostly citing workload. That changes the selection problem from organisations self-selecting in to organisations dropping out after the intervention started. It is also a reporting error in the working paper that the Institute should correct, not just a limitation.
- **Manager reports overstate output.** The manager index exceeded the records-based index in 19 of 23 organisations, a systematic and plausible bias. The comment's tone ("we do not suggest bad faith") is right.
- **Actual hours fell about 14%, not 20%.** This is a direct measurement from time-tracking logs, not an assumption.
- **Real revenue fell.** This confirms the inflation point.
- **Sectoral claims (section 5).** The point that per-hour gains are built into the metric is correct, and the Varden counter-stratum result is fairly used.

## Problems

**1. The abstract claims a correction that isn't made.**
- The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output, hours) brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours.
- Attrition is never quantified. The 61 survivors, and every subset of them, still exclude the nine withdrawals.
- A bounding analysis would give a figure for the attrition effect. For example, assign the nine organisations output of 80 (no per-hour gain), or their last observed index if one exists.
- The abstract also says four problems "account for most of the reported gain," but revenue plays no part in the per-hour calculation.

**2. Table 2 mixes corrections with changes in sample.**
- The rows use different organisations: 61, then 23, then 27, then 17. A difference between rows reflects both the correction and the change of subset.
- To separate them, show all four specifications for the same 17 organisations, starting with their manager-reported index on scheduled hours. Then the effect of each correction can be read off directly.
- The data note concedes the subsets aren't random, but the abstract and conclusion still present 10.8% as the corrected pilot result.
- No row has a confidence interval. With 17 organisations, the interval around 10.8% is probably wide.

**3. The hours breakdown doesn't add up.**
- The two sources given are +0.7 hours a day over four days (2.8 hours) and 1.6 hours on the day off, a total of 4.4 extra hours.
- Added to 32 scheduled hours, that gives about 36.4 hours a week. The table reports 34.6.
- About two hours a week is unexplained. Perhaps the +0.7 is measured against a different baseline, or part of the staff work part-time. Either the components or the total needs correcting.

**4. Record-based output is not automatically neutral.**
- One record type is "billable hours delivered." Billable hours are partly an input measure, and they fall mechanically when working time is cut, whatever happens to productivity.
- For organisations measured this way, the records-based index will understate output if work became more valuable per hour.
- The 3.8-point gap is real but may mix manager optimism with this measurement artefact. Breaking the gap down by record type would show which.

**5. The novelty argument is the weakest section.**
- Extrapolating the energy scores gives the wrong month. A straight line from 0.61 at month 3 to 0.29 at month 6 falls by about 0.107 a month and reaches zero around month 8.7, not month 10.
- More importantly, a straight line through two points is not a basis for predicting how a variable will decay. It may level off instead.
- Energy is not output. The microdata contain monthly output indices, so the direct test is available: does output per hour fall from month 1 to month 6? The comment doesn't report it. Without that, novelty is a hypothesis, not a finding.
- "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" moves the burden instead of meeting it. The comment's own conclusion is a strong claim and needs support too.

**6. Varden's case-processing result is left out.**
- It is randomised and registered, with output from administrative records and hours from timesheets. That addresses selection, the output measure and the hours denominator, three of the comment's four problems.
- It found +12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months, which is longer than the Halden pilot.
- The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature" but ignores the stratum from the same trial that cuts against its thesis. Citing one stratum and not the other is selective.
- Varden's counter stratum also found +6.7% per actual hour. As I noted on that paper, part of that may reflect fuller utilisation of staff time rather than more productive work. Still, it isn't evidence that per-hour gains are entirely artefact.

**7. Section 7 misrepresents the Varden authors.**
- They called the meetings analysis unregistered and exploratory. They said seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test. They didn't present it as a mechanism, so "should not be cited as a mechanism" argues against a claim nobody made.
- "A subgroup … selected for analysis after the results were known" is inaccurate on both counts. The seven offices are the entire treated case-processing stratum. Calendar data were collected at month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- Meeting cuts were also the most common change in the Halden interviews (47 of 58). A structural change like that is exactly the kind of non-novelty mechanism the comment needs to rule out before concluding "novelty." Dismissing it is convenient for the argument, not demonstrated.

**8. The conclusion goes beyond the evidence.**
- "Entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" doesn't follow:
  - The comment's own best estimate is a 10.8% residual gain.
  - Novelty is untested.
  - Varden shows a gain that survives randomisation and administrative measures at nine months.
- Adding "in our assessment" doesn't make the claim more modest. The overreach also extends from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.
- The second conclusion is well supported: where output depends on being present, cutting hours reduces output per employee.

## What the evidence supports

Taken together, the three documents suggest:
- The Halden headline of 23.4% was substantially inflated by misreported attrition, manager reporting and scheduled hours. In the best-measured subset the gain is about 11%, before any correction for attrition.
- Randomised evidence shows a real per-hour gain in work that can be queued (about 12%, at nine months).
- In work that depends on staff being present, the per-hour gain is small and probably reflects fuller utilisation, and service to the public declines.
- Whether gains last beyond nine months is open. Varden's 24-month follow-up, and a check of month-by-month output trends in the Halden microdata, would address that directly.

The comment's recommendations at the end are sound. Its conclusion should be revised to match its evidence, with Varden's case-processing result discussed rather than omitted.

In effect, sections 1–5 correct an overclaim and sections 6–8 replace it with an overclaim in the opposite direction.

I can draft a revised abstract and conclusion for the comment, or a short note to the Halden authors on the attrition discrepancy, if useful.
